title: Cipher Digital Starts Booking HPC Lease Revenue as $9.1B Contract Takes Shape
summary: Cipher Digital says it recognised its first high-performance-computing lease revenue in the third quarter of 2026 and extended its Barber Lake lease to 20…
content:
TL;DR: Cipher Digital says it recognised its first high-performance-computing lease revenue in the third quarter of 2026 and extended its Barber Lake lease to 20 years, increasing contracted revenue to $9.1 billion. The milestone is about converting data-centre development into an operating business, not an instant cash windfall.

A signed data-centre lease and a functioning, revenue-producing facility are not the same achievement. Cipher Digital’s third-quarter update, released November 2, places the company at an important point between those stages.

In its official business update, the company said it recorded its first high-performance-computing, or HPC, lease revenue following the start of rent at Black Pearl. It also said the lease at Barber Lake had been extended to 20 years, raising its contracted revenue value to $9.1 billion.

What first lease revenue tells us

The recognition of lease revenue shows that at least part of a project has advanced past development and into a billing relationship. It does not mean every planned data hall is operational. Cipher said multiple halls at Black Pearl and Barber Lake are scheduled to come online through year-end, so subsequent delivery remains central to the investment case.

High-performance computing infrastructure has different commercial characteristics from Bitcoin mining. Instead of purchasing machines primarily to win block rewards, the company develops sites intended to support customers’ demanding workloads under longer-term agreements. That can reduce some direct cryptocurrency market exposure while increasing dependency on construction schedules and individual tenants.

The length and total value of Barber Lake’s contract can help financiers evaluate future cash receipts. Still, contract value is not the same as revenue recognised in a quarter, cash available to shareholders or guaranteed profit. Operating expense, financing structure, maintenance and tenant performance all sit between those figures.

Energy development is becoming a competitive advantage

Cipher also reported conditional base-load classification for its 1-gigawatt Colchis project and early development of lateral pipelines intended to facilitate up to 2.5 GW of on-site generation for future expansion. These are large infrastructure ambitions, not facilities that have already delivered all their proposed capacity.

The central issue is access to reliable, affordable energy. Data-centre demand may be high, but sites cannot fulfil contracts without the supporting power network, cooling, equipment and permits. Companies that secured sites when they were focused on Bitcoin mining are trying to turn those physical advantages into AI capacity.

That shift has been a recurring theme in NewsBTC’s reporting on miners moving toward AI. Cipher’s results add a specific piece of evidence: its transition is no longer only a plan on a presentation slide, because some lease revenue has begun.

Why delivery discipline matters most

The next useful disclosures will show how much capacity has been accepted by customers, the revenue generated by each campus and the cost of completing construction. Readers should also check whether major contracts are concentrated among a small set of customers.

Cipher’s update is another reminder that Bitcoin-era data centres can develop into a very different asset class. Investors still need to judge whether the new use of that infrastructure will generate attractive returns after the enormous cost of building it. First lease revenue is a step forward, not the end of that assessment.

This article was written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

Featured image: Illustrative photograph of data-centre server cabinets (does not depict a Cipher Digital facility). Photo: PiDatacenters via Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

title: Binance CFO Exits After 5 Years to Pursue AI and Crypto Tokenization
summary: Binance Chief Financial Officer Kaiser Ng said he was leaving after five years to build ventures spanning AI, Web3, and tokenized assets. His plans covered several projects involving sports, entertainment, computing, and physical assets. Kaiser Ng Hands Over Binance’s Finance Leadership Binance Chie...
content:
Binance Chief Financial Officer Kaiser Ng said he was leaving after five years to build ventures spanning AI, Web3, and tokenized assets. His plans covered several projects involving sports, entertainment, computing, and physical assets.

Key Takeaways

  • Justin Yek will succeed Ng under a transition plan in place for six months.
  • Planned projects span basketball, music, computing, robotics, and gold.
  • Ng invited prospective team members to help pursue tokenization ventures.

Kaiser Ng Hands Over Binance’s Finance Leadership

Binance Chief Financial Officer Kaiser Ng outlined his departure and entrepreneurial plans in comments shared on X on Nov. 8, following public reports of the leadership change Nov. 7. His departure statement reflected on a decade working in digital asset exchanges. Ng stated:

“After five years as CFO of Binance, I have decided to go build something of my own.”

The departure followed Binance’s Oct. 29 hack, in which about $6.3 billion in digital assets was stolen. Binance co-CEO Yi He said the transition plan had been implemented over the preceding six months, placing the start of the plan before the attack. Justin Yek, formerly vice president of finance at payments company Airwallex, will succeed Ng.

Among those Ng acknowledged was MGX, the Abu Dhabi-based investment firm focused on AI and advanced technology. It acquired a minority stake through a $2 billion investment in Binance in March 2025. Ng also thanked the exchange’s leadership, employees, regulators, banking partners, advisers, and auditors.

Sports, Gold, and Robotics Shape His Founder Plans

Several projects featured in Ng’s next chapter, with interests ranging from basketball and music to graphics processing units, robotics, gold, and collectibles. He connected those ambitions to real-world asset tokenization and invited prospective team members to contact him. Ng stated:

“Bringing these real-world assets onto the blockchain through tokenization is a massive opportunity for the industry, and a big unlock for everyone.”

That outlook overlapped with Richard Teng’s tokenization assessment, shared in May, which highlighted regulation, institutional access, adoption, and settlement infrastructure. Teng said the following 12 to 18 months could prove defining for the sector. His assessment emphasized the systems connecting tokenized assets with regulated capital markets.

Personal interests shaped Ng’s invitation to collaborators, including his enthusiasm for basketball star Kobe Bryant. A statue of Bryant in his office had motivated him through late nights, he recalled. Ng stated: “Moving from the CFO’s chair to the founder’s is a leap, and I take it with humility.”

Binance Builds Out Tokenized Securities and AI Tools

Traditional finance assets and AI-powered interfaces featured in Ng’s account of Binance’s continued development. The exchange’s Bstocks conversion program gave eligible users a way to convert supported third-party tokenized securities into certificates backed by underlying securities. These certificates provide financial exposure without direct ownership of the underlying shares, with access and redemption subject to restrictions and product terms.

Another distribution channel opened when Ondo Global Markets joined Binance Alpha in February. Binance Alpha is a platform within the exchange’s ecosystem providing access to selected digital assets, including tokenized securities. The integration offered eligible users outside the United States economic exposure to securities including Apple, Nvidia, and Tesla.

The company’s March rollout of seven AI agent skills connected automated agents with market information, trading execution, and security analytics. Looking ahead to his own businesses, Ng described the move as an opportunity to contribute in both fields. He stated:

“I deeply believe it is where I can make a greater contribution to AI and Web3.”

title: Core Scientific’s AI Colocation Revenue Jumps to $215M as Mining Role Shrinks
summary: Core Scientific reported $215.4 million in third-quarter colocation revenue, nearly 60% above the prior quarter, while billing 485 MW of capacity. Its…
content:
TL;DR: Core Scientific reported $215.4 million in third-quarter colocation revenue, nearly 60% above the prior quarter, while billing 485 MW of capacity. Its results show how an operator once known for Bitcoin mining is building a much larger business around contracted AI infrastructure.

Some Bitcoin mining companies have talked about their artificial-intelligence ambitions for years. Core Scientific’s latest financials show what that transition looks like once facilities begin producing substantial revenue from customers.

According to its November 5 earnings release, the company generated $215.4 million of colocation revenue in the third quarter of 2026, up from $136.7 million in the second quarter and $15 million a year earlier. Total quarterly revenue reached $232.9 million.

Billing capacity is replacing hashrate as the central metric

Core Scientific said it was billing for 485 megawatts as of September 30, representing more than $700 million in average annualised colocation GAAP revenue. That is a different unit of operating performance from hashrate or Bitcoin produced. It describes contracted power and computing infrastructure delivered to tenants.

The move is important because mining revenue depends on several volatile factors at once: Bitcoin price, network difficulty, block rewards and electricity costs. Colocation can offer a different mix of long-term contracts, infrastructure obligations and construction spending. The income stream may be easier to forecast after a facility is delivered, but the capital commitment can be enormous.

Core Scientific says it is approaching full delivery under its first colocation agreement and is constructing capacity under a second agreement across five campuses. Those claims are meaningful milestones, yet remaining construction work and billing ramps still matter to the final financial outcome.

Reading the profit figures carefully

The company reported approximately $1.18 billion in quarterly net income, but said the result benefited from a non-cash change in the fair value of warrants. That makes the headline profit figure a poor stand-in for recurring cash generated by running data centres.

Adjusted EBITDA was $133.6 million, more than three times the previous quarter’s $41.1 million, while capital expenditure reached $985.1 million. Both figures deserve attention. A rapidly growing operating business can still consume substantial cash as it adds the facilities needed to earn future contracted revenue.

This is a useful counterpoint to the more familiar NewsBTC discussion of Bitcoin miners’ AI pivot. The opportunity is becoming measurable, but comparing revenue without spending, financing and delivery schedules would make the transformation look easier than it is.

What the next quarter needs to prove

Investors should follow the number of megawatts actually billing, customer diversification, operating margins, remaining capital needs and any modifications to lease terms. A nominal pipeline is less revealing than a site whose systems have been accepted by a paying tenant.

The results also offer a warning against treating every company in this sector as an identical bet on Bitcoin’s price. Core Scientific now has a material infrastructure business whose fortunes may depend more on demand for AI compute and construction execution than on daily mining profitability. Its history remains part of the story, but the metrics are changing underneath it.

This article was written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

Featured image: Illustrative photograph of data-centre server racks (Wikimedia Foundation servers; does not depict a Core Scientific facility). Photo: Victor Grigas / Wikimedia Foundation via Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY-SA 3.0.

title: Hut 8 Expands AI Campus Commitments While Funding Buybacks With Bitcoin Sales
summary: Hut 8 says it fully commercialised its Beacon Point AI campus with a second 352 MW lease, taking expected aggregate base-term contract value across its AI…
content:
TL;DR: Hut 8 says it fully commercialised its Beacon Point AI campus with a second 352 MW lease, taking expected aggregate base-term contract value across its AI data-centre portfolio to about $26.6 billion. The company also sold Bitcoin to fund share repurchases, showing how mining-era assets are being redeployed.

Hut 8’s third-quarter update is less about how many coins it mined and more about how much power, construction capacity and long-term tenant demand it can assemble. That represents a significant shift for a company long associated with Bitcoin infrastructure.

In its November 4 results, Hut 8 said a second 352-megawatt IT lease at Beacon Point fully commercialised the campus. It placed expected aggregate base-term contract value across its AI data-centre portfolio at about $26.6 billion and reported 1,330 MW of utility capacity under construction across its major AI projects.

Long leases are not the same as realised revenue

The numbers describe commitments over years, not cash that has already appeared in the bank. Hut 8’s timetable includes an initial River Bend data-hall delivery target in the second quarter of 2027, followed by Beacon Point Phase 1 in the third quarter of 2027 and Phase 2 in the second quarter of 2028.

Those future dates matter. A contracted tenant can improve the business case for a development, but execution still depends on power availability, construction, testing, financing and customer readiness. The risk profile is not identical to Bitcoin mining, where machines may be deployed in stages and production responds directly to network conditions.

Hut 8 also reported 1,300 MW of additional energy capacity entering exclusivity, bringing that category to 3,180 MW. Exclusivity is a development milestone; it should not be interpreted as an operating facility or a guaranteed utility connection. Investors need to track the movement from a pipeline into actual delivered infrastructure.

Why its Bitcoin treasury matters

The company said it bought back $74.7 million of shares during the quarter, funded with proceeds from selling approximately 954 Bitcoin. It later repurchased another $175.3 million of shares, funded through the sale of roughly 2,148 additional Bitcoin. Subsequent to the quarter, the repurchase authorisation increased to $1 billion.

That is a revealing capital-allocation decision. Selling Bitcoin to repurchase shares reduces treasury exposure to the coin while potentially increasing each remaining shareholder’s proportional interest in the company. Whether that creates value depends on the repurchase price and long-term performance of the business.

Hut 8 also closed a $1.07 billion senior secured revolving credit facility. The existence of a facility adds flexibility, but readers should distinguish committed borrowing capacity from cash revenue or money actually drawn. NewsBTC has previously examined the financing pressure created by miners’ AI expansion, and Hut 8 offers a clear example of how those choices reach the balance sheet.

The real milestones are still ahead

Hut 8 has a substantial development pipeline and named delivery targets. The crucial tests will be whether those targets are met, whether project-level financing stays on acceptable terms and how much profit flows through when sites become operational.

The update captures a broader change in listed Bitcoin infrastructure businesses. Their market stories increasingly revolve around electricity access and long-term AI customers rather than the number of Bitcoin retained. That can produce a different revenue profile, but it does not remove the need for disciplined spending or independently verifiable execution.

This article was written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

Featured image: Illustrative photograph of data-centre server racks (does not depict a Hut 8 campus). Photo: Carl Lender via Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY 2.0.

title: The Solana Company Targets Hong Kong for Massive APAC Expansion
summary: The company, which holds 2.2 million SOL, stressed that it is targeting an expansion in Hong Kong, as the city has identified tokenization as a key area of fintech development. The expansion could increase the company’s headcount to 30 people to potentially serve local banks. Solana Company Aims To ...
content:
1. News
  2. Finance
  3. The Solana Company Targets Hong Kong for Massive APAC Expansion

Published:Nov 8, 2026, 7:30 PM EST

The company, which holds 2.2 million SOL, stressed that it is targeting an expansion in Hong Kong, as the city has identified tokenization as a key area of fintech development. The expansion could increase the company’s headcount to 30 people to potentially serve local banks.

WRITTEN BY

SHARE

Published: Nov 8, 2026, 7:30 PM EST

Key Takeaways

  • The Solana Company is expanding its tokenization services to Hong Kong to capitalize on Asia’s fintech growth.
  • Designated as a strategic enterprise, the firm plans to build a 30-person local team to advise institutions.
  • This move bolsters Hong Kong’s financial ecosystem, integrating new local stablecoins onto the Solana network.

Solana Company Aims To Expand in Hong Kong Amid Tokenization Surge

As Asia and China open to real-world asset tokenization (RWA), companies are starting to aim at these regions as expansion hubs for their operations.

The Solana Company, a publicly traded organization that holds 2.2 million SOL, valued at nearly $197 million, is looking at Hong Kong to expand its tokenization services platforms, as the city has classified the activity as a key area of fintech development.

Joseph Chee, chairman and CEO of the Solana Company, referred to the APAC (Asia-Pacific) region as the “biggest opportunity for Solana” during an interview, according to SCMP.

While the Solana Company is technically a Digital Asset Treasury (DAT) for Solana, focusing on accumulating and maximizing its SOL per-share numbers by leveraging capital markets and blockchain activity, the organization will build infrastructure and provide tokenization services as more and more companies seek advice on these processes in Hong Kong.

While Hong Kong’s tokenization journey is just starting, regulators have already greenlit 17 tokenized retail products with assets under management (AUM) calculated at $1.3 billion, up over a third from last year.

Chee stressed that while Hong Kong is growing, the U.S. leads the industry and is “moving a lot faster,” with regulators even approving venues for stock tokenization. “A lot of major financial institutions in Hong Kong are just starting to think about or initiate a tokenization project,” he assessed, and he believes that the company might assess demand for these services in six months.

If demand holds and no large teams rise locally to satisfy it, the company aims to grow its headcount to 30 and build a local team to offer tokenization services to local banks.

Chee’s statements come after the Solana Company was designated as a strategic enterprise by the Hong Kong Government’s Office for Attracting Strategic Enterprises (OASES) as part of its seventh batch of strategic enterprises.

At the time, Chee stressed that Hong Kong would become “the base from which we will advise institutions and build infrastructure across the region,” and that the Solana Company was looking forward to “exploring how digital asset infrastructure can contribute to Hong Kong’s financial institutions.”

As part of its digital assets push, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) has already approved two companies, HSBC and Anchorpoint, to launch Hong Kong dollar stablecoins, with the latter planning to offer native token issuance and redemption on the Solana blockchain.

About the author

WRITTEN BYSergio Goschenko

Sergio is a cryptocurrency journalist based in Venezuela with 2,000+ articles published, cited in dozens of papers and reports.

title: Riot Sells More Than 20,000 Bitcoin as AI Data-Centre Contracts Reach $38B
summary: Riot Platforms says it sold 20,264 BTC in the first nine months of 2026, raising about $1.5 billion primarily for data-centre development. Its latest…
content:
TL;DR: Riot Platforms says it sold 20,264 BTC in the first nine months of 2026, raising about $1.5 billion primarily for data-centre development. Its latest quarterly release puts long-term contracted data-centre revenue at around $38 billion, underlining how far the miner’s business model is shifting.

Riot Platforms has made a striking choice with its Bitcoin holdings: sell a substantial amount of the asset it mines to finance the infrastructure it hopes will deliver future revenue. That strategy is clearer than ever in its third-quarter results, released November 4.

In its earnings filing, Riot said it sold 20,264 Bitcoin year to date for approximately $1.5 billion, mainly to fund data-centre construction. The company also announced a 15-year powered-land lease for 910 critical IT megawatts at its Corsicana campus, representing about $28 billion of contractual value over the initial term.

Mining remains substantial, but contracts tell the new story

Riot recorded $181.4 million in third-quarter revenue, barely above the comparable quarter a year earlier. Bitcoin mining contributed $116 million, down from $160.8 million, even though production increased to 1,637 BTC from 1,406 BTC. The company attributes much of the decline in mining revenue to a lower average realised Bitcoin price during the quarter.

At the same time, engineering revenue rose to $47 million and data-centre revenue was $18.4 million. Those lines make the transition visible in the income statement, although the extraordinary long-term lease figures are not the same as cash already earned. They depend on delivery milestones, counterparties, the terms of each agreement and years of operations.

Riot says it has now leased 1,151 MW of critical IT capacity, with roughly $38 billion of long-term contracted revenue. Investors should distinguish that total contract value from current profit, and consider what future capital expenditure may be required to bring the facilities online.

Why selling Bitcoin is a strategic trade-off

The Bitcoin sales create resources that can fund land, power connections, construction and specialised infrastructure. They also reduce direct exposure to future Bitcoin appreciation. It is a deliberate decision to exchange part of a liquid treasury asset for a business with potentially steadier contracted revenues, but one that carries construction and customer concentration risks.

Riot said it ended September with $950.2 million of cash and Bitcoin, including 2,418 BTC. It reported no equity raised during 2026, a detail relevant to shareholders concerned about dilution as build-outs expand.

Mining economics are still important. Riot reported an average cost to mine Bitcoin of $39,265 excluding depreciation, influenced by power-curtailment credits. Such credits are valuable, but energy arrangements and pricing can change. Our earlier look at Bitcoin miners’ growing AI commitments explored the same industry-wide tension between holding coins and building something new.

What will show whether the pivot works

The milestones that matter most are construction progress, delivery of contracted megawatts, tenant payments and conversion of headline lease values into recurring revenue. A business can accumulate an impressive contract pipeline while facing sizeable financing, permitting or execution obstacles.

Riot’s disclosure shows that Bitcoin mining companies are not necessarily behaving like Bitcoin holding companies. One of the industry’s biggest operators is increasingly using the mined asset as a funding source for a different kind of data-centre business. That may eventually diversify earnings, but the timing and profitability have to be proven in cash flow rather than headlines.

This article was written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

Featured image: Illustrative photograph of Bitcoin mining racks (2018 Argo Blockchain Mirabel facility; does not depict a Riot Platforms site). Photo: MikeBogosian via Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

title: Coinbase Explains Cold-Storage Defences After Binance Breach Shakes Crypto Industry
summary: Coinbase says it was not affected by the reported Binance hot-wallet incident and that more than 99% of customer assets are kept in cold storage. The…
content:
TL;DR: Coinbase says it was not affected by the reported Binance hot-wallet incident and that more than 99% of customer assets are kept in cold storage. The exchange outlined controls around signing, withdrawal limits and suspicious activity, offering a useful test of how custodians should explain security practices.

A major attack on one exchange inevitably prompts customers elsewhere to ask the same question: where are my assets actually held, and what stops them being moved without permission? Coinbase addressed those concerns in a November 4 security explanation, published against the backdrop of the reported Binance incident.

In its official post, Coinbase said it had not been affected by the breach and that more than 99% of customer assets were held in cold storage. It also described distributed signing keys, withdrawal limits, anomaly detection and emergency controls capable of stopping transaction signing.

What cold storage protects, and what it does not

Cold storage refers broadly to arrangements designed to keep signing authority away from routine internet-connected systems. It can reduce the exposure of a custodian’s largest reserves if a hot wallet or application layer is compromised. Hot wallets remain useful for normal withdrawals, so the balance between operational liquidity and offline custody matters.

The reported percentage is Coinbase’s stated current practice; it should not be interpreted as a universal guarantee that every customer balance is insulated from every type of problem. Account takeover, internal controls, fraud, software defects and legal restrictions are separate categories of risk. A security system is strongest when the organisation explains the entire chain of access rather than relying on one impressive percentage.

Similarly, distributed keys can mean that no single compromised system can authorise a large movement, but only if the policy around those keys is well implemented. Limits and anomaly detection add further layers, potentially buying time when a transaction looks unusual.

Why the industry is revisiting wallet architecture

Custodians face an awkward operational challenge. Users expect transfers to work continuously, but allowing automated movement from the internet-connected part of a system increases the consequences of a compromise. A good model therefore combines preventative controls with monitoring and rehearsed incident procedures.

The disclosure comes as industry participants investigate the reported multi-billion-dollar Binance exploit and as stablecoin issuers describe the actions available to them once assets have left a platform. These are connected but distinct defences: custody aims to stop unauthorised signing, while downstream tracing and freezes aim to limit damage after funds move.

The importance of resilience is also visible in decentralised finance. As NewsBTC reported when Aave restricted new tBTC supply and borrowing, operational controls can reduce further exposure during an incident. They are most useful when their scope is explicit and their effect is independently checked.

What exchange users should ask

Useful questions include whether balances are fully backed, what proportion is held in internet-connected wallets, how withdrawals are approved, whether controls are independently assessed, and how the company communicates if access is interrupted. A customer should also understand the difference between assets held by a platform and tokens in a wallet whose private keys they personally control.

Coinbase’s statement offers concrete details rather than simply calling itself secure. Those details still need to be assessed over time against audits, incident disclosures and actual operational performance. The wider lesson is that custody design belongs at the centre of an exchange’s risk story, not in small print below a trading app.

This article was written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: Vitalik ‘pivots’ ETH to store of value, crypto suffers after US midterms: Hodler’s Digest
summary: Vitalik Buterin wants Ethereum to embrace a store of value narrative, upsetting Bitcoin maxis. The crypto industry faces an uncertain future following the US elections.
content:
Ethereum creator says ETH should be valued as an SoV

Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin says the network should promote ETH as a store of value, rather than as an asset that derives value from burning fees.

He argued in a thread that idea of “ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed” and that optimizing for that would negatively impact Ethereum’s “decentralization and capture resistance.”

Instead, he argues that Ethereum’s value should come from stability provided by its focus on “decentralization and CROPS” — referring to censorship and capture resistance, open source, privacy and security — which he believes will be more highly valued in an “era of AI disruption.”

The 2021 EIP-1559 upgrade flipped Ethereum into deflationary mode for a time when fee revenue was sky high, leading to supporters, including the Bankless podcasters, touting Ethereum as “ultrasound money.”

But due to design choices, fees have kept falling along with revenue, making that narrative unsustainable. From January to October this year median transaction fees fell from 35 cents to 3.5 cents, as the number of daily transactions increased by more than half.

Some Bitcoiners, who hold BTC’s store of value status sacred, were scathing about Buterin’s thread. Held Media founder Dan Held derided Buterin’s comments as “ETH trying to pivot to Bitcoin’s SoV narrative after all of its previous narratives collapsed. Again.” He argued it was “wild that you think a protocol with a constantly changing monetary policy (just like fiat) can be a ‘sound money.’” However, proponents note that Ethereum has not changed its monetary policy since The Merge in 2022, and each change has reduced, rather than increased, issuance.

Ethereum maxis welcomed the protocol’s creator setting a clear narrative direction. MetaLeX attorney Gabriel Shapiro called it a “nature is healing moment” from Buterin, and said “I think on fundamentals ETH can be a much better SoV than both ZEC and BTC.”

Even Solana co-founder Anatoly Yakovenko said Buterin was “absolutely right that can’t focus on fees as the product” although he then took a subtle dig at Ethereum’s “product.”

Source: Toly

Democrat sweep spells uncertain future for crypto regulations

Despite spending $176 million across 100 seats — including $64 million trying and failing to keep Sherrod Brown out of the Senate — the influence of crypto super PACS on the election appeared to be minimal. Or was it?

Even though the Democrats now control both the Senate and the House of Representatives a Fairshake spokeman told Crypto In America the super PAC had spent $154.5 million across 93 races and backed the winning candidate in all but seven races. That’s a 92% success rate.

Stand With Crypto notes that majorities of legislators in both houses are now pro-crypto, with 50 of 100 senators designated “pro-crypto” and only 33 “anti-crypto,” while 241 congress people support the industry, and only 106 actively hate it.

However the anti-crypto army will hold positions of power, with Brown likely to join the Senate Agriculture Committee and Elizabeth Warren tipped to chair the Senate Banking Committee.

“The next Congress will bring a fundamentally different environment for crypto in Washington, and the industry should expect significantly more scrutiny,” said Kyle Bligen, executive director at the Decentralization Research Center.

Democrats are already reportedly considering expanding proposals from Representative Maxine Waters into a broader market structure bill. There is still an outside chance the CLARITY Act could be resurrected, but only if it has much stronger ethics provisions aimed at President Donald Trump’s alleged corruption.

“A sitting president’s family launching memecoins and a stablecoin is a real governance problem,” Fidelity Digital founder Hadley Stern told Magazine. “If I’d done that at Fidelity, I’d have been walked out the same afternoon.”

The TRUMP memecoin lost a third of its value this week, and was the biggest loser in the top 100 cryptocurrencies.

The election result saw AI related stocks crash and Bitcoin fell below $76,000 where it remains.

Fake job interview led to Binance’s $6.34 billion hack

Binance reports that North Korean hackers first breached its systems back in June, when an employee downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation while attempting to install an AI coding tool. While the exchange quickly detected the incident, the hackers had already obtained information about employees working on Binance’s wallet infrastructure.

In September, attackers posing as recruiters targeted another software engineer and tricked the employee into downloading a malicious file disguised as a coding assignment.

On Oct. 20, the attackers used the compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain access to two additional engineers’ systems to deploy malware. They then gained access to the exchange’s internal wallet-signing service, enabling them to steal billions.

“This wasn’t one mistake or one breach — it was a months-long campaign,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said in a Tuesday post on X.

Ethereum dev targets 2028 for quantum resistance, a year early

Ethereum Foundation researcher Justin Drake is targeting December 2028 to complete Ethereum’s post-quantum and post-AI transition, a year earlier than the foundation’s previously announced quantum-resistance deadline.

Speaking at Devcon 8 in Mumbai on Tuesday, Drake outlined the accelerated timeline. “Our hope is that by December 2028 we’ll be able to wrap up the full post-quantum and post-AI transition,” Drake said, adding that developers have 24 months to deliver three additional network upgrades.

The Ethereum Foundation’s September roadmap established December 2029 as its deadline for achieving quantum resistance.

However the roadmap is currently at a standstill with core developers delaying the Glamsterdam upgrade indefinitely until security concerns tied to eight smart contract invariants are resolved.

THORChain restarts despite FBI warning

THORChain has ignored the FBI’s explicit warning not to process funds from the Binance hack, with the permissionless protocol restoring trading on most networks on November 4.

The RUNE token gained 15% in 24 hours on the news that Bitcoin, Ethereum, Bitcoin Cash, Dogecoin, Litecoin, Tron and Zcash had been re-enabled. Avalanche, Base and XRP were already operating.

Chainalysis reported that THORChain had already processed more than $46 million from the hack in the first 72 hours, and gained $200,000 in fees according to the Wall Street Journal. Trading was halted automatically due to an unrelated Ethereum block reorganization.

Co-founder JPThor said the fact that the FBI warning had no effect on the DEX proved that THORChain was decentralized.

“The fact that the FBI did in fact call out the protocol —— and nobody could do anything —— means in fact the protocol is decentralised. Nobody in their right mind in a western country would flagrantly ignore a direction like that.”

Winners and Losers

At the end of the week, Bitcoin (BTC) is down 4.5% to trade at $74,302, Ethereum (ETH) is down 6.3% to trade at $2,117 and XRP (XRP) is down 5% to $1.11. The total market cap is at $2.49 trillion according to CoinMarketCap.

Among the biggest 100 cryptocurrencies, the top three altcoin winners of the week are Pieverse (PIEVERSE) with a 39.2% gain, Injective (INJ) on 11.1%, and Tether Gold (XAUt) on 4.2%.

The top three altcoin losers of the week are OFFICIAL TRUMP which was down 32.8%, Worldcoin (WLD) down 20.8% and Ethena (ENA) down 19%.

Top Prediction of the Week

Binance hack may be ‘temporary setback’ for crypto, Grayscale’s Pandl says

Binance’s $6.3 billion hack could temporarily hurt confidence in crypto markets but would ultimately lead to stronger security practices across exchanges, according to Grayscale.

“It also underscores the importance of institutional custody, such as offered by US-based crypto [exchange-traded products],” said Grayscale’s head of research, Zach Pandl, in a Tuesday report.

“These vehicles hold their assets at state-chartered banks and qualified custodians, typically offering offline storage, multi-signature wallets, SOC attestations and insurance policies,” he added.

Top FUD of the Week

Binance France emails announce closure of its users’ accounts on Dec. 31

Binance France is closing up shop in the country. All accounts will be closed on Dec. 31, and any assets left on the exchange will be charged monthly fees starting on Nov. 29, according to emails sent to users by Binance.

On that date, accounts still maintaining a balance will pay a monthly maintenance fee of 0.025% of the balance, or a minimum of 10 USDC, a stablecoin tracking the US dollar.

Cointelegraph reported in late June that Binance had notified European Union users access to key services would be restricted after the exchange failed to secure Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) regulatory authorization from a member state before a July 1 deadline.

Suspicious prediction market activity seen before election poll release: NYT

Suspicious prediction market bets were placed shortly before two recent New York Times/Siena political polls were released to the public, according to a report.

Vanderbilt University researchers said a Polymarket user bet almost $200,000 on Oct. 31 that Nebraska Senator Pete Ricketts would be re-elected. An hour later, a Times/Siena poll was released showing Ricketts in the lead.

A Friday New York Times report said while it was not clear if the user had access to inside information, they won more than $77,000. The user also placed similar large bets on other markets, including Kalshi, the report said.

Gnosis Pay breach exposes personal and card details

Crypto-linked Visa debit card provider Gnosis Pay disclosed a security breach on Friday that exposed customers’ payment card details, home addresses and cryptocurrency wallet addresses.

Gnosis Pay said it detected unauthorized access to its legacy consumer card system on Nov. 3 and began containing the breach within two hours. The company said customer funds and its separate enterprise platform, which powers white-label card programs, were unaffected.

The CLARITY Act faces a new test as Democrats control Congress, raising questions over consumer protections, ethics and what the crypto industry may have to concede.

Bitcoin holders have received eCash — What can you do with it?

Bitcoin’s eCash fork gives eligible holders an equivalent balance of ECX, but questions remain over where they can trade the tokens and what they can do with them.

title: Jensen Huang Admits Affair as Nvidia Probes Alleged Chinese Spy Plot
summary: Jensen Huang’s admission of infidelity has collided with an Nvidia board investigation, suspected Chinese espionage and congressional demands for answers.
content:
Skip to content
Assets: NVDA

Jensen Huang’s admission of infidelity has collided with an Nvidia board investigation, suspected Chinese espionage and congressional demands for answers.

The Jensen Huang affair has reached Nvidia’s boardroom. The company is opening an independent investigation into reports that its chief executive was targeted by foreign intelligence, while Huang has admitted being unfaithful to his wife. A private betrayal now sits alongside questions about a major chip customer and suspected Chinese espionage.

The November 8 announcement puts Huang’s personal judgment under scrutiny alongside a larger question: whether access to one of technology’s most influential executives created a national-security risk. Nvidia’s board says it currently has no reason to believe company secrets or U.S. national security were compromised.

The Jensen Huang affair: a private betrayal becomes public

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” Huang wrote in an employee message seen by Reuters.

In the fuller message published by Bloomberg, Huang described the love and support he had received from his family and acknowledged damaging the life they had built together. The admission makes the consequences personal even as Nvidia’s directors examine questions of corporate security.

The apology is unusually personal for a corporate crisis. It acknowledges harm to his family while employees, customers and investors confront the implications of the reports surrounding their chief executive. The intimate admission and the security investigation are linked by the reporting, but they answer different questions.

Bloomberg reported that Huang, 63, will remain CEO while the inquiry proceeds. It identified the woman at the centre of the reports as Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, whom U.S. authorities suspect was recruited by a Chinese spy agency.

Huang had previously described his contacts with Megaspeed employees to Bloomberg as typical business relationships. His admission of infidelity now sits alongside that earlier account, intensifying questions about where customer access ended and personal intimacy began.

Nvidia backs its founder while opening an inquiry

A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent lawyers, will oversee the review. Nvidia said Huang supports the investigation and has committed to cooperating.

The board said it has “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” while promising to examine all available information. It also expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team.

That leaves the company balancing two difficult messages: its founder retains the directors’ backing, but the allegations warrant an independent examination. The announcement gave no timetable for completing the inquiry.

An affair admission does not establish that Huang knowingly assisted an intelligence operation or disclosed sensitive information. The investigation’s findings, rather than the most dramatic descriptions of the relationship, will determine what the board can substantiate.

Who is Alice Huang, and why does Megaspeed matter?

Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are not related. The Associated Press, citing New York Times reporting, described her as a Chinese citizen and chip buyer who became a senior executive at Megaspeed, a significant Nvidia customer in Southeast Asia.

The commercial relationship gives the story stakes beyond a CEO’s private life. In an October 29 statement, Senator Elizabeth Warren cited reporting that Megaspeed had bought at least $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia chips.

Warren’s demand was direct: “NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang and NVIDIA’s board owe Congress answers.”

However, the responses from governments do not form a single, uncontested account. China rejected the earlier espionage allegations, according to SBS’s report on an October 30 foreign-ministry briefing.

Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs issued a separate clarification on October 31: it denied that Singapore officials had expressed the reported concerns about Alice Huang or conducted such investigations into her. An accompanying police response confirmed that an investigation into Megaspeed was ongoing.

The distinction matters. An inquiry into a company’s activities is not proof that one of its executives worked for an intelligence service.

Congress wants a closed-door explanation

Three Republican House committee chairs have already requested a joint briefing on Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s protections against foreign espionage.

Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, who lead the Foreign Affairs, China Select and Intelligence committees respectively, proposed November 18. They asked Huang to accept that date or offer another congressional session date by November 11.

“It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk,” the chairmen wrote.

The request is for a briefing, not an announced finding of wrongdoing. It nevertheless places Huang’s explanations before lawmakers whose concerns extend from personal access to the protection of advanced American technology.

A personal crisis at the centre of the AI race

Huang’s influence reaches beyond chip sales. BNC has previously examined his role in Washington’s debate over open AI models, where Nvidia’s commercial interests intersect with arguments about American technological leadership.

The immediate test is whether the independent review can establish what information, if any, was exposed and whether safeguards were sufficient. For shareholders, continued leadership is only part of the issue; confidence in the company’s controls matters too.

For Huang, the consequences are public and personal. He has acknowledged betraying his family while continuing to lead Nvidia through an investigation whose security questions remain unresolved. The apology is on the record. The intelligence allegations still require answers.

title: Binance Restores HYPE, APT as Data Reveals Billions in Reserve Outflows
summary: Binance restored withdrawals for the altcoins hyperliquid (HYPE) and aptos (APT) on Sunday, Nov. 8, advancing its recovery from the $6.3 billion October hack. Meanwhile, Cryptoquant’s latest exchange metrics reveal substantial declines in bitcoin, ethereum, and stablecoin reserves, even as daily wit...
content:
Binance restored withdrawals for the altcoins hyperliquid (HYPE) and aptos (APT) on Sunday, Nov. 8, advancing its recovery from the $6.3 billion October hack. Meanwhile, Cryptoquant’s latest exchange metrics reveal substantial declines in bitcoin, ethereum, and stablecoin reserves, even as daily withdrawal pressures appear to be easing.

Key Takeaways

  • Binance reopened HYPE and APT withdrawals on Nov. 8, ahead of its previously announced target.
  • Cryptoquant data shows Binance’s bitcoin reserves falling approximately 56,000 BTC since before the hack, while ethereum holdings declined roughly 400,000 ETH.
  • Ethereum-based stablecoin reserves have contracted by approximately $9 billion, although recent daily flows suggest withdrawals are stabilizing.

Binance Withdrawal Recovery Advances After Historic $6.3 Billion Hack

The cryptocurrency exchange continues to gradually restore services following the Oct. 29 attack, which saw approximately $6.3 billion stolen from hot wallets across multiple blockchains. The incident, attributed by blockchain investigators and U.S. authorities to North Korean hackers, ranks as the largest cryptocurrency theft recorded in dollar terms.

On Sunday, Binance announced:

“Latest Withdrawal Update. Withdrawals have now been re-enabled for the following networks and assets: HYPE, APT.”

The announcement followed Binance’s Nov. 6 commitment to restore withdrawals for HYPE, APT, INJ, PLASMA, NEAR, and LTC by the end of the following week. The first two assets returned ahead of schedule, while other withdrawal routes remain subject to individual security assessments.

Binance initially resumed withdrawals on Nov. 1, reopening access to major cryptocurrencies across 15 networks. The exchange subsequently expanded support to dozens of additional assets, including tokens operating on Ethereum and Solana.

Although the recovery has progressed, onchain evidence offers a more revealing examination of the financial consequences.

Cryptoquant Shows Bitcoin Reserves Down 56,000 BTC

According to Cryptoquant metrics examined through Nov. 8, Binance’s bitcoin reserves have fallen from approximately 730,000 BTC before the attack to 673,700 BTC, representing a decline of roughly 56,000 BTC, or 7.7%. At bitcoin’s current price of $75,800 on Sunday, that difference represents approximately $4.2 billion in holdings.

The most pronounced withdrawals occurred between late October and early November, when daily bitcoin netflows registered approximately negative 14,500 BTC, 22,000 BTC, 16,500 BTC, and 9,000 BTC.

The 22,000 BTC withdrawal reading marked the largest daily net outflow across the 12-month stats. However, subsequent activity included a positive 10,400 BTC session, suggesting the initial selling and withdrawal pressures were beginning to dissipate.

The latest reading shows approximately 1,300 BTC in positive daily netflows, a considerable improvement from the extraordinary movements recorded immediately after withdrawals resumed. Ethereum’s numbers tell a somewhat harsher story.

Binance’s ethereum reserves declined from approximately 3.48 million ETH to 3.08 million ETH, a reduction of 400,000 ETH, or 11.5%. Two particularly severe daily netflow readings approached negative 175,000 ETH and 155,000 ETH. The latest daily ethereum netflow remained negative at approximately 5,500 ETH.

Stablecoin Reserves Take the Hardest Proportional Hit

The most conspicuous deterioration appears in Binance’s Ethereum-based stablecoin reserves, which declined from approximately $41 billion before the attack to $32 billion by Nov. 8. That represents a significant contraction of approximately $9 billion, or 22%, substantially exceeding the proportional declines recorded for bitcoin and ethereum.

Binance Stablecoin ReservesAmount
Before Oct. 29 hack$41 billion
Nov. 8, 2026$32 billion
Total decline$9 billion
Percentage decline22%

Two daily stablecoin net outflows approached $3.3 billion and $3.6 billion, roughly triple the largest comparable daily withdrawal previously recorded during 2026. Nevertheless, the latest daily reading showed positive stablecoin netflows of approximately $27.9 million, indicating that the extraordinary withdrawal activity has moderated.

These reserve declines should not be confused with Binance’s previously reported $3.64 billion in net customer withdrawals, equivalent to approximately 2.1% of reported assets. Cryptoquant’s measurements include movements associated with the theft and the Binance hacker, alongside this, the analytic firm’s stablecoin figures cover Ethereum-based tokens rather than every blockchain.

Earlier investigations likewise documented exceptional withdrawal activity following the reopening, alongside evidence that the initial exodus was losing momentum.

Arkham’s $162.65 Billion Snapshot Offers Another Perspective

At the time of writing, blockchain analytics platform Arkham Intelligence places Binance’s labeled cryptocurrency holdings at approximately $162.65 billion across 68.5 million addresses. Its Nov. 8 metrics identify roughly 696,184 BTC and 3.454 million ETH, exceeding Cryptoquant’s respective estimates by approximately 22,500 BTC and 374,000 ETH.

Different wallet attribution methods, blockchain coverage, and reporting methodologies can produce discrepancies between a myriad of analytics providers in 2026. Nevertheless, both datasets identify substantial reserve reductions following the October attack.

Meanwhile, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic recently reported that the attackers converted approximately $174 million in stolen alternative cryptocurrencies into another 2,300 BTC, expanding their bitcoin holdings. Binance reported Nov. 4 that approximately 98% of affected assets had been replenished, with remaining purchases complicated by limited token liquidity.

The central question now extends beyond restoring individual withdrawal services. Binance’s latest flow readings suggest the immediate exodus is subsiding, but its diminished reserves illustrate the financial consequences still visible across the exchange. Operational recovery and the restoration of confidence are related achievements, though the available evidence does not establish that either process is complete.

title: Bitcoin Faces CPI Test After AI Stock Sell-Off
summary: Bitcoin faces October’s U.S. inflation report after the AI stock sell-off, with Tuesday’s CPI release and CoreWeave results testing appetite for risk.
content:
Skip to content
Assets: BTC

Bitcoin faces October’s U.S. inflation report after the AI stock sell-off, with Tuesday’s CPI release and CoreWeave results testing appetite for risk.

Bitcoin faces a fresh inflation test on November 10 after an AI-led sell-off exposed how quickly pressure in technology stocks can spill into crypto. The next question is whether U.S. price data will ease interest-rate concerns or give investors another reason to retreat from risk.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release October’s consumer price index at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday. Later that day, AI cloud provider CoreWeave reports quarterly results, putting monetary policy and the economics of the AI boom in focus within hours of each other.

AI stock losses put Bitcoin’s recovery under pressure

The setup follows a sharp reversal in sentiment. In its November 6 market update, CoinShares said the previous day’s trading saw the Nasdaq fall 5.5%, the Nasdaq-100 lose 6.4% and semiconductor stocks drop 12%, while Bitcoin declined just over 5%.

More than $1 billion in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated during the sell-off, according to the update. Bitcoin miners with growing exposure to AI and data centres were particularly vulnerable, illustrating how diversification into computing infrastructure can also tie their fortunes more closely to technology stocks.

CoinShares’ head of research, James Butterfill, argued that interest rates and liquidity remained central to Bitcoin’s outlook following the U.S. midterm elections.

“The election changes the political backdrop, but the Fed still holds the more important cards,” he wrote.

The Bitcoin CPI test: look beyond the headline number

The inflation backdrop is already uncomfortable. The September CPI report showed consumer prices rising 0.6% over the month and 3.7% over the year. Gasoline prices jumped 9.1%, accounting for more than half the monthly headline increase.

Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% month-on-month and 2.6% year-on-year. That distinction matters for Tuesday: a slowdown driven mainly by cheaper energy would offer different information from a broader cooling in underlying prices.

Investors will therefore need to examine the monthly core reading and the composition of inflation, alongside the annual headline rate. Comparing the release with market expectations will be more informative than treating any decline from September as an automatic signal to buy.

The October numbers are not available yet. The chart shows the published historical backdrop, including the renewed acceleration in monthly headline inflation through August and September.

The Fed has already signalled caution

The Federal Reserve held its policy rate at 3.75%–4% on October 28, but the decision was not unanimous. Two officials preferred a quarter-point increase.

“Inflation remains elevated,” the committee said, adding that further information would help determine the appropriate policy stance.

The labour market has since added another consideration. The October employment report, released November 6, showed payrolls increasing by 165,000 and unemployment at 4.1%. Those figures give policymakers fresh evidence to weigh alongside inflation before their December 8–9 meeting.

What hotter or cooler inflation could mean for Bitcoin

A stronger-than-expected inflation reading could reinforce expectations of tighter policy. If Treasury yields and the dollar rise in response, Bitcoin could face renewed pressure as investors reassess the appeal of holding riskier assets.

A softer report, especially one showing less persistent core inflation, could support the opposite reaction. Lower rate expectations could improve the conditions for a recovery in crypto and technology shares.

Neither outcome guarantees a particular Bitcoin price move. These are scenarios for interpreting the release, and positioning matters: an apparently favourable number can produce a muted response if traders have already anticipated it.

The useful confirmation would come from several markets moving together. A Bitcoin rebound accompanied by easing bond yields and firmer technology stocks would tell a different story from a brief crypto spike that fades while financial conditions remain tight.

CoreWeave adds a second test for the AI trade

Inflation is only the first event on Tuesday’s calendar. CoreWeave has scheduled its third-quarter earnings call for 5 p.m. Eastern Time on November 10.

Its results and commentary could offer another window into AI infrastructure demand, financing needs and the pace of data-centre expansion. One company cannot settle the wider debate over AI valuations, but the timing gives investors a separate source of information after the inflation report.

That matters for Bitcoin because last week’s selling showed that crypto can be caught in a wider reduction in risk exposure, even when the immediate concerns originate outside digital assets.

What to watch after the release

Brave New Coin’s recent Bitcoin market analysis identified the $73,000 region as an important downside reference and $79,000–$80,000 as an area of resistance. Those are reference levels from that analysis, rather than forecasts of where CPI will send the market.

Tuesday’s immediate test is whether inflation changes the interest-rate outlook enough to shift risk appetite. The stronger signal will be whether Bitcoin can sustain its response once the first burst of volatility passes—and whether the AI earnings news reinforces or challenges that move.

title: Circle Says It Froze $1.1B in USDC Linked to Binance Hack Investigation
summary: Circle says it froze roughly $1.1 billion in USDC connected with the reported Binance exploit while working with law enforcement. The stablecoin issuer…
content:
TL;DR: Circle says it froze roughly $1.1 billion in USDC connected with the reported Binance exploit while working with law enforcement. The stablecoin issuer stresses that a wallet freeze does not decide asset ownership or whether funds should ultimately be forfeited.

The response to the enormous reported Binance breach has exposed a difficult but essential distinction in digital finance: tracking money is not the same thing as freezing it, and freezing it is not the same thing as recovering it for a victim.

In a November 5 statement, Circle said it had frozen approximately $1.1 billion in USDC associated with the incident, in coordination with law enforcement. It described an attack involving more than $6 billion in digital assets, while emphasising that the investigation and identification of relevant funds remain ongoing.

Why USDC can be frozen when Bitcoin cannot

USDC is issued by a company that operates an administratively controlled token system. Under certain legal processes, the issuer can freeze specified addresses so tokens cannot move in or out. Bitcoin, by contrast, does not have an issuer with an equivalent global address-freezing switch. That difference can matter enormously in the first minutes after an attack.

But it also raises governance questions. Who is authorised to request a freeze? What evidence is required? How quickly can an incorrect restriction be lifted? Circle says it acts on valid legal process and does not decide for itself whether a crime occurred, whether a wallet’s owner committed an offence or who is entitled to the assets. Those questions belong to law enforcement and the courts.

This makes it important not to count frozen funds as already returned to customers. A frozen balance may remain subject to lengthy investigations, ownership disputes and judicial decisions. The amount is an intervention figure, not a completed reimbursement total.

The race between cross-chain transfers and enforcement

Modern crypto breaches move across bridges, exchanges, token pairs and custody services. Attackers may split assets among many addresses and convert one token into another to make intervention harder. Defenders need analytics capable of tracing flows across those boundaries, along with responsive institutions that can take action where legal powers exist.

An earlier NewsBTC report on Aave freezing new tBTC activity illustrated how different controls can be used to reduce exposure within a protocol. Circle’s move is not the same kind of action, but both show why the ability to intervene is a design choice with trade-offs.

For investigators, the key issue is coordination. An address identified in one jurisdiction may be connected to a stablecoin issuer or exchange in another. Delays can give attackers more time to swap tokens and fragment holdings. Moving quickly is therefore useful, but speed cannot replace careful identification and due process.

What is still unknown

The full scope of the incident, ultimate recoveries and allocation of any frozen funds will require additional verified disclosures. Blockchain traces alone can also create false impressions when commentators assign an address to a person without sufficiently strong evidence. Circle’s account is an issuer’s report of its own intervention, not an independently completed forensic audit of every transfer.

The development offers a lesson beyond this incident. Dollar stablecoins can provide rapid payment settlement and targeted interdiction, yet their compliance controls concentrate important operational powers in issuers. Users, institutions and regulators need to understand both sides of that bargain.

This article was written by the News Desk and edited by Samuel Rae.

title: Samsung Wallet Adds USDC Purchases Through Stripe
summary: Samsung Wallet’s USDC purchase integration with Stripe brings digital dollars to eligible U.S. Galaxy users, expanding stablecoin access through a familiar mobile wallet.
content:
Skip to content
Assets: USDC

Samsung Wallet’s USDC purchase integration with Stripe brings digital dollars to eligible U.S. Galaxy users, expanding stablecoin access through a familiar mobile wallet.

Samsung Wallet USDC purchases are now powered by Stripe, giving eligible Galaxy users in the United States a way to buy the dollar-pegged stablecoin through a familiar mobile app.

In a November 5 announcement, Stripe said its Crypto Onramp supports purchases in the Samsung Wallet Stablecoin Account across 82 million compatible U.S. Galaxy devices. Customers can buy USDC using Samsung Pay, credit and debit cards, or ACH bank payments.

That figure describes the potential device footprint, rather than 82 million registered accounts or active stablecoin users. Stripe did not disclose customer numbers, purchase volumes or transaction activity in its announcement.

How Samsung Wallet USDC purchases work

Stripe said its onramp “handles identity verification, compliance, and fraud prevention” as part of the purchase. Samsung Pay is also now available to other businesses using Stripe’s Crypto Onramp, extending the payment option beyond Samsung’s own stablecoin account.

For consumers, the practical change is the entry point. Buying digital dollars through a wallet already on a phone could make the first transaction less intimidating than opening a separate crypto exchange account. The commercial opportunity rests on whether that easier start translates into repeat payments and transfers.

Samsung’s stablecoin rollout began before Stripe’s announcement

The November update follows Samsung’s October 7 announcement, which scheduled the feature’s launch for the final week of that month. Stripe’s news identifies the purchase infrastructure supporting that rollout.

“Sending money abroad should feel as convenient as using the wallet already on your phone,” said Woncheol Chai, Samsung’s executive vice president and head of its Digital Wallet Team, in the October announcement.

Samsung described transfers to compatible crypto wallets and eligible bank accounts in more than 60 countries, with bank recipients receiving local currency. It also identified Bastion as an infrastructure provider and Coinbase as the sub-custodian securing USDC through Coinbase Prime Vault.

Samsung says it charges no fee for USDC transfers to supported external wallets, although receiving services can apply their own charges and network conditions affect speed. Bank remittances have a different fee structure, varying by destination and amount, with costs and estimated delivery times displayed before confirmation.

Samsung listed future online and in-store stablecoin payments as possible additions. Those plans should be distinguished from the funding and transfer capabilities being offered now.

Who can use the Samsung Wallet Stablecoin Account?

According to Samsung’s current FAQ, users must be at least 18 and live in an eligible U.S. jurisdiction. New York residents are currently excluded. Compatible devices need Android 13 or later and enabled fingerprint authentication.

The account supports holding, sending and receiving USDC, international remittances and optional rewards. Dollar deposits are converted into USDC, with withdrawals converted back into dollars.

Samsung says the account “holds digital assets, not bank deposits.” Balances and rewards lack FDIC, NCUA and SIPC protection. There is no account-opening fee, but funding, withdrawal and transfer costs depend on the method and destination; other providers may levy separate charges.

These details matter when comparing the feature with existing payment services. Convenience alone does not establish that a particular transfer will be cheaper. The relevant comparison is the total amount paid by the sender against what arrives at the destination.

Why distribution matters for stablecoin adoption

USDC issuer Circle reported approximately $69.2 billion in circulation as of November 5. Circle says the token is backed by liquid cash and cash-equivalent reserves and is redeemable one-for-one for U.S. dollars.

On its reserve transparency page, Circle says reserves are held separately from its operating funds and that it publishes weekly reserve disclosures alongside issuance and redemption flows. A major accounting firm provides monthly assurance on reserve coverage. Those disclosures offer a way to examine the backing of the token independently of announcements about new wallet integrations, although they do not measure how widely any individual wallet is used.

That structure gives USDC a different purpose from assets such as Bitcoin: it is designed to track the dollar, rather than offer exposure to a rising cryptocurrency price. Reserve backing, however, is a separate question from the protections and terms of a consumer wallet account.

Brave New Coin has previously examined how stablecoin adoption depends on reach and financial infrastructure. Samsung’s integration provides a concrete example of that distribution strategy: put access to digital dollars where consumers already manage other payment tools.

The potential advantage extends beyond attracting existing crypto holders. A person looking to send money abroad may care more about the recipient’s payout, the fee and the delivery time than the blockchain used behind the scenes. A useful product has to satisfy those needs consistently.

The next test is usage

The rollout offers a substantial distribution channel, but its success will require evidence beyond device compatibility. Account activation, repeat transfers and transaction volumes would help show whether customers see lasting value in the service.

For now, Stripe’s involvement establishes how eligible Samsung users can fund their stablecoin accounts. The next milestone is whether those purchases become a routine part of moving money, rather than a feature customers try once and leave unused.

title: Fhenix – Privacy on a Need-to-Know Basis
summary: Guy Itzhaki is CEO of Fhenix, a fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) company whose CoFHE coprocessor lets smart contracts on existing EVM chains compute over encrypted data without users moving to a new chain. Itzhaki spent much of his career at Intel, where he took its SGX and TDX trusted execution e...
content:
Skip to content

Guy Itzhaki is CEO of Fhenix, a fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) company whose CoFHE coprocessor lets smart contracts on existing EVM chains compute over encrypted data without users moving to a new chain. Itzhaki spent much of his career at Intel, where he took its SGX and TDX trusted execution environments to market and later led its FHE and blockchain initiatives, with a stint as a technology advisor for the Tokyo and Paris Olympic Games, before joining founder Guy Zyskind to launch Fhenix three years ago.

The link will open a new window. Click the menu and down arrow to download the file.

Guy Itzhaki is CEO of Fhenix, a fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) company whose CoFHE coprocessor lets smart contracts on existing EVM chains compute over encrypted data without users moving to a new chain. Itzhaki spent much of his career at Intel, where he took its SGX and TDX trusted execution environments to market and later led its FHE and blockchain initiatives, with a stint as a technology advisor for the Tokyo and Paris Olympic Games, before joining founder Guy Zyskind to launch Fhenix three years ago.

Why you should listen

For as long as most engineers have worked with encryption, encrypted data has been unusable until it is decrypted, whether in the open or inside secure hardware. Itzhaki, who spent years selling that secure-hardware approach at Intel, says the moment of decryption is where the risk lies, which is why FHE has long been called the holy grail of cryptography. The math has existed since Craig Gentry’s breakthrough more than 15 years ago, but FHE was dismissed as too complex for anyone but specialist cryptographers and too slow for production. Itzhaki argues both objections are now largely answered. Developers building on Fhenix don’t need to understand the cryptography at all, and faster algorithms running on GPUs, and eventually dedicated ASICs, keep improving performance. CoFHE went live on Ethereum and Arbitrum mainnet in October. Itzhaki sees Web3 as only the first market, and expects private queries to AI models to become feasible within two to three years.

The more interesting part of the conversation is how Fhenix found its market. The company started as a privacy-focused Layer 2, then concluded the world didn’t need another public chain and rebuilt itself as a coprocessor for chains developers already use. It spent its early days testing gaming, NFTs and meme coins before settling on the area where privacy matters most: financial assets moving between parties, especially stablecoins and tokenized assets. Itzhaki separates confidentiality from anonymity. Fhenix keeps senders and receivers visible so KYC and AML still work, and hides only what is in the transaction. A permit system lets an asset owner grant decryption rights to an auditor, a compliance officer or a regulator, which puts onchain data on a need-to-know basis. A dual token standard lets a single ERC-20 switch between a public mode for DeFi and a private mode for balances and payments. Early design partners show the range of uses: AlphaEngine lets traders keep strategies encrypted while liquidity providers see only a performance score, Obolos puts company cap tables and compliance rules onchain, and Fluton is building confidential payments, swaps and trading.

Itzhaki is candid about the competition. He credits Zama with proving there is real demand for onchain privacy, and notes that Fhenix absorbed Sunscreen, the third early FHE team, in July. He says Fhenix differs in three ways: a second FHE scheme planned for next year, its dual token SDK, and support for EVM chains generally rather than a single chain. He also previews fUSD, a confidential token due in about a month, whose staked version, fUSDY, is meant to earn yield through partners, so private balances can still be put to work. The hot take round covers his firmest conviction that privacy matters and institutions are coming, a ten-year outlook in which AI agents run most onchain activity, and a warning that quantum attacks may arrive within roughly two years, much sooner than most people assume. He closes by admitting he is a Lord of the Rings maximalist.
